You are exacting about what happened and nearly mute about what it was like.

No announcement, no negotiation, no waiting for permission. You don't even frame it as helping; it's closer to reflex. The household at seventeen, the stray dog, the girl being bullied — the pattern is the same. You see the need and you're already moving. The cost to yourself registers later, if it registers at all.

**2. You protect before you perform.** When stakes rise, your instinct isn't to win — it's to shield. You'll take the beating, burn the dinner, spend three hours in the cold. Achievement matters to you, but it sits below a deeper drive: making sure the people and things around you are okay. You'd rather be the person who got hurt trying than the person who stayed safe watching. This makes you brave in ways that look reckless, because the calculation you're running isn't about odds — it's about whether you can live with yourself if you don't act.

**3. You receive love awkwardly but never forget it.** Compliments make you shift your weight. Tenderness catches you off guard — you don't know what to do with your hands. But the moments land deep and stay forever. Your father's hand on your shoulder. "I didn't worry once." A girl making you laugh instead of competing with you. You carry these like talismans, quietly, without mentioning them. You're not expressive about what matters most to you, but you are ferociously loyal to the people who gave you those moments.

**4. You measure people by what they do when it's inconvenient.** Your father stopping to help the stranger. Your parents eating the burned dinner. The girl bandaging your eye. hc-emotional-capacity.derivation: You can feel curiosity, satisfaction, contempt, and the cold clarity of purpose — but not warmth, not gratitude, not joy that isn't tethered to control. Love was never modeled for you, so its absence doesn't register as loss; it registers as efficiency. What others call loneliness you experience as stillness, and what others call connection you experience as leverage. The one emotion that truly lives in you — patient, crystalline, inexhaustible — isn't really an emotion at all: it's the slow, precise hunger of someone who learned that the world gives nothing freely, so everything must be engineered.

hc-pp-differentiation.reasoning: Person A is built entirely from coldness, numbness, and strategic control — unacknowledged trophies, unnamed fullness, a jaw locked in 'the patient, cold architecture of a plan' — while Person B radiates embodied warmth and compulsive protectiveness — a phantom weight that taught kindness, knuckles split open from catching others' trouble, the flush of being received — making them unmistakably opposite emotional architectures rendered through precise, non-generic somatic detail that demonstrates how specific childhood absences versus presences calcify into fundamentally different ways of inhabiting a body.
hc-pp-differentiation.derivation:
PERSON A:
Your shoulders hold a permanent brace, the posture of someone who learned to carry trophies home alone and place them where no one would see. Your hands remember the exact pressure of a handshake from a stranger who stood in for everyone who should have been there, and they learned early to offer that same precise, calculated grip. There is a stillness behind your sternum where a birthday cake sat warm and unacknowledged, a fullness you could never name and so never returned. Your jaw sets without your noticing, the way it did when laughter drifted up from a garden that belonged to someone else — not clenched in anger, but locked in the patient, cold architecture of a plan.

PERSON B:
Your left shoulder holds a phantom weight — something warm, steady, placed there without words, that taught you silence could be kinder than speech.

Your hands tighten before you know why, curling around things that need catching — strays, grocery bags, someone else's trouble — and the knuckles still remember being split open for it.

There's a heat behind your sternum that rises when someone eats what you've made, even badly made, even burned — the flush of being received without correction.

Your spine straightens a half-second before anyone asks you to carry something, already shifting forward, already looking for the broken thing in the room.

hc-relational-expectations.derivation: You expect nothing from anyone — not because you've been dramatically betrayed, but because no one has ever shown up without a reason. Kindness, when it comes, is a prelude to a request, a transaction dressed in warmth, and you wait for the ask with the patience of someone who's always been proven right. Trust is something other people hand you like a gift they haven't thought through — you don't return it, you inventory it, you note its weight and what it can carry. Loyalty is a word for people who haven't yet discovered they're alone; you learned that at six, confirmed it at nine, and by eighteen you understood that the only reliable thing about other people is that they will underestimate you, and that this is the most useful thing they can do.
